title: Row overfetch turned into row-wide LDPC in sense-amp stripe
idea: Reverse the 128x overfetch from waste into an asset: every ACT already senses a full 8 Kb row, so an XOR-tree LDPC check (~3% parity over the whole row) runs in the sense-amp stripe at activation, instead of SECDED per 64 b at the I/O. The row-wide code corrects 40+ bit errors per row, so cells with raw BER ~1e-4 (smaller Cs, longer refresh) become shippable.
why: Capacitor charge wall + refresh: tolerating 1e-4 raw BER allows ~30-40% smaller Cs or ~4x refresh interval; parity overhead falls from 12.5% to ~3%.

title: Asymmetric Z-channel codes for one-way charge-loss errors
idea: Flip the symmetric-error assumption: retention and hammer errors in true-cells are almost all 1->0, so the array is built with true-cells only (no anti-cells) so every cell leaks toward the same logical value, and SECDED is replaced by unidirectional-error codes (Bose-Lin / Z-channel LDPC) that need fewer check bits per corrected error.
why: Retention tail + row hammer: ~2x correction strength per parity bit vs symmetric codes, letting refresh interval stretch ~2x at equal reliability.

title: Charge-sparse constant-weight encoding so most cells hold zero
idea: Reverse which state carries information: each 64 b word is encoded into an 80-cell constant-weight codeword with only ~25% charged cells, so ~75% of cells sit in the discharged state that cannot leak or be hammered; any 1->0 flip changes the weight, giving free detection.
why: Retention-vulnerable cells and hammer exposure drop ~2-3x and write energy falls; the ~25% capacity cost is repaid by permitting cheaper, weaker cells and longer refresh.

title: Lifetime-matched retention: data expires before the cell forgets
idea: Flip refresh to follow the data's lifespan instead of the cell's: AI activations, KV-cache blocks and network buffers declare a time-to-live at allocation and land in a refresh-free region whose cells only guarantee ~5 ms retention; the controller refreshes only lines whose TTL outlives that window.
why: Refresh (16-33% idle power, 10-20% bandwidth) eliminated for short-lived data, and that region can use low-AR capacitors with ~3x less charge.

title: Weak cells hold only clean pages, re-fetched on error
idea: Rearrange placement by dirtiness: pages with an intact copy in flash or CXL far memory (weights, code, read-mostly caches) go to cheap weak-retention DRAM protected only by a 16-bit CRC, and a CRC failure triggers a re-fetch instead of correction; a line is migrated to strong ECC banks on its first write.
why: Lets ~60-80% of inference-server capacity use reject-grade or long-refresh cells; ECC overhead on that share drops from 12.5% to ~3%.

title: Spare-free dies: host controller owns all row repair
idea: Reverse who owns redundancy: DRAM dies carry no spare rows, fuse banks or address comparators; failing rows found at test go into a signed manifest and the host memory controller remaps them through an on-SoC 64 KB CAM into a host-reserved pool, one remap fabric serving dozens of dies.
why: Periphery is ~49% of die: removes ~3-5% die area of redundancy/fuses plus fuse-blow test time; yield loss becomes a small capacity haircut.

title: Skip fab retention test; profile retention in customer racks
idea: Reverse the test order: dies ship after a short functional test, skipping the hours-long hot retention screen and burn-in; on first boot and weekly thereafter the controller runs retention-pattern sweeps during idle and bins each row into refresh classes stored in module NVRAM.
why: Test capex and cycle time cut ~30-50%; per-row refresh binning cuts refresh energy ~50-70% vs worst-case refresh.

title: Inverted HBM stack puts logic base die beside the lid
idea: Rearrange the stack so the hot base/logic die sits on top against the heat spreader and the DRAM dies sit below next to the interposer, with signals using the same through-stack TSVs; DRAM layers leave the logic die's heat path and run ~8-12 C cooler.
why: Retention roughly doubles per ~10 C, so refresh rate and retention-tail failures halve, or weaker cells are accepted at the same refresh.

title: In-array analog activation integrator replaces digital hammer counters
idea: Move hammer tracking from periphery into the array: each row gets one extra tiny cell that receives a fixed charge packet through a diode-connected path on every activation and slowly leaks; when its voltage crosses a threshold during the row's own sensing, a flag triggers refresh of both neighbors, with the leak rate setting the time window.
why: Row hammer at ~1k activations: per-row tracking for ~0.01-0.1% area instead of SRAM/CAM counters that cost several % of die and do not scale.

title: Quarantine hot aggressor rows inside a moat subarray
idea: Flip mitigation from victims to aggressors: a row exceeding the hammer threshold is migrated into a small quarantine subarray where every occupied row is flanked by two never-used guard rows, so further hammering finds no victims; it migrates back when it cools.
why: Row hammer: replaces repeated victim refreshes (bandwidth tax) with one migration; costs ~0.5% capacity for the moat.

title: Skewed cross-bank row mapping scatters hammer victims across codewords
idea: Rearrange the address map so a logical row is built from physical rows at different indices in each of 8 banks (index = L XOR bank-hash); a hammered logical row disturbs a different logical victim in each bank, so any victim word gets errors in at most one 1/8 slice, which a per-slice symbol code corrects.
why: Row hammer: raises the effective uncorrectable-flip threshold ~8x with no counters; costs only address-hash logic.

title: Idle-time self-hammering maps each row's true flip threshold
idea: Reverse attacker and defender: in idle windows the controller copies a row aside, hammers it with known patterns, records the activation count at first flip, and programs per-row thresholds into mitigation logic, re-running as the chip ages.
why: Row hammer: most rows tolerate far more than the worst-case 1k, so tailored thresholds cut mitigation refreshes ~5-10x.

title: Sense-amp latch time as soft information for LDPC
idea: Reverse decide-then-correct: a time-to-digital counter on each sense-amp group records how long the latch took to resolve; slow resolutions mean small signal and are tagged low-confidence, and a soft-decision decoder (Chase / min-sum LDPC) flips the least-confident bits first.
why: Capacitor charge wall: soft decoding gains ~1.5-2 dB over hard decisions, tolerating ~30% less sense signal (smaller Cs or longer refresh).

title: Memory that trades capacity for parity as it ages
idea: Rearrange the parity/data split over the product lifetime: modules start with ~2% parity, and as the error log shows a region degrading, the controller re-encodes it with a stronger code and hot-unplugs the freed pages from the OS, degrading gracefully instead of failing.
why: Extends module service life ~2x and lets fabs ship cells that are weaker at end of life; fewer replacements raise usable supply.

title: Test-reject DRAM dies sold as graded AI cache memory
idea: Reverse the reject bin into a product line: dies failing retention or hammer specs are packaged into 'Grade-R' modules with published per-row maps, sold for KV caches and recomputable buffers with host software ECC and short-TTL use at ~40% of prime price.
why: Raises usable bit supply by recovering several % of wafer output now scrapped or down-binned, with zero new fab capex.

title: Tensor checksums replace DRAM ECC for model weights
idea: Flip error checking from memory to compute: weight matrices carry row/column checksums (algorithm-based fault tolerance), the GEMM verifies them, and a mismatch re-fetches that tile from a peer GPU or flash; the weight region in DRAM drops ECC entirely.
why: Removes 12.5% ECC overhead for AI's largest data class and tolerates ~1e-6 raw BER weak cells; checksum cost <1% of FLOPs.

title: Wordline Joule pulses anneal retention traps in the field
idea: Reverse aging into healing: during maintenance windows a bank goes offline and high current is driven through segmented wordlines (far end shorted by a switch) to heat the local array to ~250-300 C for milliseconds, annealing the trap states behind variable-retention-time cells.
why: Retention tail / VRT: could cut tail cells ~2-5x and rejuvenate aged parts, allowing longer refresh intervals.

title: Electron recapture pulse after aggressor activation bursts
idea: Reverse the hammer charge flow: after N activations of a row, the drivers apply a brief opposite-polarity pulse to the neighboring passing wordlines and local well contact to drift injected electrons back toward the aggressor's drain before they reach victim storage nodes.
why: Row hammer: if electron migration is the dominant path, the flip threshold could rise 5-10x with no refresh bandwidth spent.

title: Corrected-error patterns detect hammer instead of activation counting
idea: Reverse cause and effect: rather than counting activations, the controller spatially correlates corrected-error syndromes from scrubs and reads, using planted canary rows holding worst-case patterns; correctable flips clustering in rows R+1/R-1 identify R as an aggressor to throttle.
why: Row hammer: near-zero-area mitigation tuned to real chip vulnerability, suited to low-cost parts or as a backstop to counters.

title: Row-embedded fault patch list replaces fuse repair
idea: Rearrange repair data into the row it fixes: each 8 Kb row reserves ~32 bits holding up to two (column-address, correct-bit) patches, and the column path applies them on the fly at read, fixing single-cell defects without spare rows or fuses.
why: Single-cell hard faults dominate yield loss; in-row patching cuts redundancy area and lets ~10x higher single-cell defect density ship.

title: Write first, compute on-die parity later in idle
idea: Reverse write ordering for on-die ECC: partial writes land immediately without read-modify-write, affected codewords are marked parity-stale in a small SRAM bitmap, and parity is recomputed at the next activation or idle slot, accepting a microsecond-scale unprotected window.
why: On-die ECC read-modify-write costs DDR5 up to ~10-20% write bandwidth; this recovers it while keeping protection for data at rest.

title: Vertical parity row rebuilds any dead row per subarray
idea: Rearrange ECC from horizontal to vertical: each subarray keeps one parity row equal to the XOR of its ~512 rows, with write deltas accumulated in an SRAM buffer and flushed during refresh, so a broken wordline, hammered row or stuck row is rebuilt as an erasure.
why: Turns whole-row failures into correctable erasures for ~0.2% overhead, allowing cheaper, less perfect wordline processing.

title: Cluster hot pages together so neighbors refresh themselves
idea: Reverse OS page placement: instead of spreading hot pages, the allocator puts frequently activated pages in physically adjacent rows so every potential victim is itself activated (and restored) about as often as its aggressor, keeping cold data out of the hot zone.
why: Row hammer: victims self-refresh, cutting mitigation refreshes ~5x for typical access patterns at zero hardware cost.

title: Three low-aspect capacitors vote as one via triple-row activation
idea: Reverse one strong cell into three weak ones: with fluorocarbon high-AR oxide etch banned, capacitors are built at ~20:1 in an amorphous-carbon mold patterned by O2 plasma (ZrO2 from amide ALD, TiN from TiCl4); each bit is written to 3 rows and read by activating all 3 at once, so charge sums on the bitline and one failed cell is outvoted.
why: Capacitor charge wall without PFAS etch: 3 x ~1.7 fF gives a 5 fF-class signal plus built-in single-cell fault tolerance; density cost is offset by far cheaper low-AR etch.

title: Self-clearing capacitor electrodes burn away dielectric weak spots
idea: Borrow film-capacitor self-healing and reverse what fails: the top electrode is ultrathin TiN from TiCl4/NH3 ALD (no WF6, no NF3 cleans), and a controlled overvoltage pulse at test vaporizes electrode around any leakage spot in the ZrO2, isolating the defect while ~99% of the capacitor stays active.
why: Retention tail from dielectric weak spots (higher with fluorine-free chamber cleans): converts leaky cells into good ones, shrinking the tail ~3-10x.

title: Parity mat per bank absorbs particle killers from NF3-free cleans
idea: Flip yield from fab to array: chambers are cleaned with remote H2/O2 or Cl2 plasma instead of NF3, accepting more particle killers, and each bank adds a parity mat equal to the XOR of its 16 data mats in the same activation, so a particle-killed mat is reconstructed on the fly without fuse repair.
why: Removes NF3 while holding yield; tolerates one dead mat per bank for ~6% area.

title: Shared per-template repair map for repeating imprint defects
idea: Reverse per-die repair into per-template repair: nanoimprint litho with a non-fluorinated release layer (alkylsilane or diamond-like carbon instead of perfluorosilane) repeats template defects at identical coordinates on every die, so each template is inspected once and its defect map is mask-programmed into ROM remap logic on all dies it prints.
why: Makes capital-light, EUV-free imprint patterning viable by turning its worst weakness (repeating defects) into a one-time repair; cuts per-die test and fuse time.

title: Voltage-accelerated room-temperature retention test replaces fluid-chilled testers
idea: Reverse the stress axis: instead of heating and chilling test heads with perfluoropolyether heat-transfer fluids, retention screening runs at room temperature with raised cell-node, plate and negative-wordline bias that accelerates junction and GIDL leakage by a calibrated factor equivalent to 85-95 C.
why: Removes PFAS fluids from ATE and cuts thermal soak time ~5x, lowering test capital per bit.

title: Hydrocarbon-refrigerant chilled memory tier that barely refreshes
idea: Flip from refreshing hot memory to chilling it: a capacity-tier DRAM shelf is held near -20 C by propane (R290) or CO2 (R744) vapor-compression loops instead of HFC refrigerants or fluorinated immersion fluids, stretching retention ~1000x so refresh drops to seconds.
why: Refresh power and bandwidth nearly removed and cells with ~10x lower Cs become usable; chiller power offsets part of the gain.

title: Twin landing-pad contacts survive stochastic misses from PFAS-free resists
idea: Rearrange each storage-node contact from one landing pad into two half-size pads in parallel: tin-oxo metal-oxide EUV resists without fluorinated photo-acid generators print more stochastic missing contacts, but a cell now fails only if both pads miss, squaring the defect rate.
why: Contact stochastic failure falls from ~1e-7 to ~1e-14 per cell, allowing PFAS-free resists without yield loss for a few % area.

title: Buried electron-sink line between rows soaks up hammer charge
idea: Give hammer electrons somewhere else to go: a shallow trench cut with HBr/Cl2 (no fluorocarbons) between adjacent rows is filled with in-situ boron-doped epi (avoiding fluorine-bearing BF2 implants) and biased slightly positive to collect migrating electrons before they reach victim storage nodes.
why: Row hammer threshold possibly raised 10x+ without counters or refresh; costs ~5-10% cell area.

title: Passivate last: high-pressure deuterium anneal after every plasma step
idea: Reverse the order and swap the passivant: instead of fluorine incorporation in gate and junction oxides, the finished wafer gets a final ~20 atm D2 anneal after all plasma and BEOL steps so no later damage undoes it, and Si-D bonds resist hot-carrier breakage far better than Si-H.
why: Interface-trap junction leakage and VRT tail cut ~2x, recovering fluorine's reliability benefit with no fluorine.

title: Grow the junction first, pattern it later with chlorine ALE
idea: Reverse implant-then-pattern: the access-transistor junction is grown as an in-situ-doped, graded phosphorus/arsenic epi stack (no BF2) before patterning, then cut with Cl2/Ar atomic-layer etching, giving a low-field, implant-damage-free junction.
why: GIDL and trap-assisted tunneling dominate the <=13 fA leakage tail; lower peak field and no implant damage could cut the tail ~3x.

title: Rows switch to twin-cell mode when HF-free cleans leave leaky cells
idea: Rearrange two single cells into one differential cell on demand: wafers cleaned without HF (ozone water, SC1/SC2, H2 bake) show more leaky-tail cells, so at boot the controller switches only rows containing tail cells into 2T2C mode, pairing them with a neighbor row storing the complement on BL/BLB.
why: Differential pairs tolerate ~10x more leakage; applied to only ~1-3% of rows, capacity loss stays small while enabling a fully HF-free front end.

title: TSV-free stacks with coded inductive links replace Bosch-etched TSVs
idea: Reverse copper wiring into magnetic fields: since Bosch deep-silicon etch needs SF6/C4F8, stacked DRAM dies communicate through on-chip coil pairs across thinned silicon, with a lightweight link FEC and retransmission absorbing coupling errors.
why: Attacks the HBM TSV tax (~3x area per bit, 20-30% yield loss): no TSV keep-out zones or TSV yield loss, and fully PFAS-free stacking.

title: Field error telemetry tunes chlorine etch recipes back at the fab
idea: Reverse the information flow: modules stream anonymized per-row error and retention telemetry tagged with die IDs to the fab, where it trains recipe corrections for the less mature Cl2/HBr and O2 etches replacing fluorocarbon steps, closing the yield loop in weeks instead of quarters.
why: Speeds yield learning for a PFAS-free process ~2-3x, making the constraint economically survivable.

title: Center-tapped wordlines for chloride-precursor molybdenum fill
idea: Rearrange the wordline driver from the end to the middle: buried wordlines filled with Mo from MoO2Cl2 (replacing tungsten from WF6) are driven from a center tap, halving RC so far-end cells get a full restore within tRAS.
why: Under-restored far-end cells feed the retention tail; also removes WF6 and dependence on China-concentrated tungsten.

title: Map bf16 mantissa bits onto weaker pitch-walk bitlines
idea: Rearrange data significance onto process asymmetry: fluorine-free spacer patterning (non-PFAS resists, Cl/HBr/O2 etches) enlarges SAQP pitch walk so alternate bitline sets are systematically weaker; the controller maps sign/exponent bits onto strong lines and low mantissa bits onto weak lines without ECC.
why: AI tensors tolerate low-mantissa errors, so larger pitch-walk variation is accepted without yield loss or extra patterning precision.

title: Etch slow to leak less: chlorine atomic-layer channel recess
idea: Reverse the throughput priority: the recessed-channel access transistor trench is cut by self-limiting Cl2/Ar atomic-layer etching, one monolayer per cycle, instead of fast fluorine plasma, flattening channel depth variation to ~1 nm.
why: Tighter Vt and lower trench-corner field compress the leakage tail ~2x so refresh can relax; slower etch adds tool time but zero fluorine.

title: Nonvolatile fault-map sidecar remembers weak cells across power cycles
idea: Rearrange where reliability knowledge lives: a small MRAM chiplet patterned by argon ion-beam etching (no fluorinated chemistry) is co-packaged with each DRAM stack and stores per-row retention classes, hammer thresholds and patch lists, so profiling survives power-off and travels with the module.
why: Makes field profiling, per-row refresh and host-owned repair practical without re-profiling at every boot.

title: Shared plate line reads a row's popcount as a checksum
idea: Reverse plate and bitline roles for detection: the plate electrode of each row segment (TiN from TiCl4) is sensed during activation, and its displacement charge is proportional to the number of charged cells, giving an analog popcount compared against a stored count to flag flips without per-word parity bits.
why: Error detection for ~0.5% overhead vs 6-12% ECC parity, freeing area for larger-footprint, fluorine-free low-AR capacitors.

title: Fine-tune each model to its own DRAM's fault map
idea: Reverse adaptation: instead of repairing memory to fit the model, each deployed model is briefly fine-tuned with weights forced to zero at the exact stuck or weak bit positions of the DRAM it occupies, absorbing the higher defect density of a fluorine-free fab.
why: Ships dies with ~1e-5 hard-fault density for inference at <0.1% accuracy loss and no repair area.

title: First-boot forming pulse punches through HF-free contact oxide
idea: Reverse a defect into an antifuse: without HF dips, contacts keep ~0.5-1 nm of chemical oxide that creates a resistance tail; at first power-up a controlled forming pulse breaks down that thin oxide only in contacts flagged as slow-writing, turning them ohmic.
why: Contact-resistance tails cause write and restore failures; a one-time electrical fix enables an HF-free front end.

title: Spare hybrid-bond pads with bit-steering for plasma-activated bonding
idea: Rearrange the bond interface into a repairable bus: HF-free surface prep (N2/O2 plasma activation, water rinse) leaves more bond voids, so each 32-pad group carries 2 spare pads and a bit-steering mux, configured at stack test, that routes around open pads.
why: Keeps hybrid-bonded DRAM stack yield above ~99% despite higher void density, cheaper than TSV-stack yield loss.

title: Rest banks under deep reverse bias to undo chloride-gate BTI
idea: Reverse stress into recovery: chlorine-precursor TiN gates may add trap-driven Vt drift, so the controller rotates banks through scheduled recovery intervals with access transistors held at a deeper-than-standby negative gate bias, de-trapping charge before the leakage tail grows.
why: Prevents aging-driven growth of the leakage tail and keeps refresh intervals stable over the product life.

title: PFAS-free certified DRAM grade paired with system-level ECC
idea: Flip the constraint into a market: define a certified PFAS-free DRAM grade for public buyers and hyperscaler sustainability targets, specified at relaxed raw BER and retention and sold with mandatory system-level ECC and per-row refresh, so new fabs without fluorinated steps can sell from day one.
why: Raises supply from simpler new fabs, pre-empts the proposed EU universal PFAS restriction and strengthens US manufacturability.
